477.title: Omniscience — and the invitation of the gods, refused (3.49–3.51)
477.hook: discernment brings knowing everything, and the next step is letting even that go; then the gods arrive with an invitation, and the yogi says no
477.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often tell the Bhashya's scene of the gods' invitation to warn students against both attachment and pride in their progress, and Hindu stories praise renunciants who turn down heavenly rewards for the sake of liberation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: indriya-jaya, the senses. From the known to the knowing; today, the knower.

The classical commentary tells it as a scene. A yogi sits in practice, far along now, close to the end. And the gods arrive. Not demons, not tempters in disguise. Gods, the beings of the high places, warm and respectful. Sir, sit here. Enjoy yourself here. This pleasure is lovely. This elixir holds back age and death. Here's a chariot that flies. Here are trees that grant every wish. Come and stay. Generous, polite, and sincere. Today's sutras say what the yogi does next.
screen: `THE GODS ARRIVE.` → `SIT HERE. ENJOY HERE.` → `COME AND STAY.`

segments.voice: First the summit. Sutra 3.49: for the one who sees only the difference between the mind's clearest part and the seer, mastery over all states of being, and knowing everything. Omniscience. Sarva-jnatritva. This is discernment, met three weeks ago, carried all the way. Then sutra 3.50, a bold line. By dispassion even toward that, the seeds of every fault are destroyed, and freedom comes. Kaivalya. Even omniscience gets set down. Then 3.51. When invited by those in the high places, don't be attached, and don't be proud, because unwanted things could return. Two dangers, not one. Attachment: you might say yes. And pride: you might say no, and then think, the gods themselves came to invite me. The commentary gives the yogi's answer as a reflection. I've been roasted on the coals of rebirth, tossed in the dark, and now I've found the lamp of yoga. Why would I let these sweet things be the wind that blows it out? So the yogi refuses. Quietly. No speech, no triumph. Notice who's at the door. Not enemies. Gods, and good things: long life, beauty, ease. A generous invitation can be harder to turn down than a hostile one. And on an ordinary Tuesday? The invitation is rarely a flying chariot. It's the comfortable stopping place, just short of what you set out to do.

segments.voice: Rest on the breath until something pleasant invites you away, a daydream, a plan for later, a drowsy warmth, and notice it like a kind visitor at the door. Thank it silently and stay with the breath. If a little pride follows at having stayed, greet it the same way, and let it pass.
Omniscience. Knowing everything, which comes from full discernment, and which Patanjali says to let go of too.
Your line: refuse the invitation. Kindly, without clinging to it, and without pride. Rest well.

478.title: Discernment of the moment (3.52–3.54)
478.hook: samyama on the single instant and the order of instants brings the knowledge that carries you across
478.tomorrow: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self
478.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study 3.52–3.54 with the classical commentary's account of the instant, and in meditation practitioners often train attention on the present moment of the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: omniscience, and the invitation refused. The gods at the door, declined without clinging and without pride.

Two gooseberries sit on a table. Same size, same green, same tiny freckle near the stem. You look at them, then step out of the room. While you're gone, someone swaps them. You come back. Which is which? Nothing on the surface says. The classical commentary uses this very puzzle to explain today's sutras. Its answer: someone with the right kind of discernment could tell them apart. Not by color or shape. By time.
screen: `TWO IDENTICAL GOOSEBERRIES.` → `SWAPPED WHILE YOU WERE OUT.` → `WHICH IS WHICH?`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.52: by samyama on the moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discernment. The word for moment is kshana, the instant. As the atom is the smallest piece of matter, the commentary says, the instant is the smallest piece of time. And sequence, krama, is just instants following one another without a break. Then something startling. An hour, a day, a year: those are put together by the mind. They don't exist out there as things. Only one instant is real at a time. The whole world changes in that single instant, and past and future are carried in it as what has been and what will be. Sutra 3.53: from this, you can tell apart two things that look the same, that share kind, marks and place. The two gooseberries. Each one has its own line of instants, its own history, moment after moment. Rest samyama on that, and the swap is plain. Sutra 3.54 names this knowledge. Taraka, the one that carries across, like a ferry over a river. It takes everything as its object, in every way, and it's without sequence. All at once, not one thing after another, the way the mind usually knows. So book three's tour of powers ends here, not with flying or vanishing, but with seeing the single instant clearly. And there's an ordinary version. Much of what weighs on a person is an hour, a week, a year, piled up in the mind. The instant itself is often light.

segments.voice: Notice the breath, not this breath as a whole, but this instant of it, the tiny touch of air right now, then this one, then this one. When the mind builds something bigger, the rest of the day, the week, notice the building and come back to this single instant, light as it is.
Taraka, the knowledge that carries across, like a ferry over a river. By samyama on the instant and its sequence, this is what discernment of the moment becomes.
Your line: the instant. Only one is real at a time. That's day four seventy-eight.

479.title: Kaivalya — when purity of mind equals purity of self (3.55–3.56)
479.hook: the book of powers ends not with a power but with a cleaned window: when the mind is as pure as the seer, there is freedom
479.tomorrow: The powers by birth, herbs, mantra, discipline, samadhi
479.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, kaivalya is the goal of practice: the seer standing free of entanglement with nature, reached through discernment and dispassion, and teachers stress that it does not depend on gaining any powers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taraka, the knowing that carries across, and the single instant, light as it is.

Somewhere there's a sliding glass door so clean that people walk straight into it. The glass is still there, still holding the weather out. But it adds nothing of its own to the garden beyond: no smudge, no tint, no reflection of the room. You see only what's there. Book three has spent fifteen days on powers. Its last sutra isn't a power at all. It's that door.
screen: `A GLASS DOOR SO CLEAN.` → `PEOPLE WALK INTO IT.` → `IT ADDS NOTHING OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: The last sutra of book three: when the purity of the mind's clearest part equals the purity of the seer, kaivalya. The mind's clearest part is sattva, the quality of light and clarity. The seer is purusha, pure awareness, which never needed cleaning. So all the work is on one side: the glass, not the garden. Practice, discernment, letting go, all of it wipes the glass until it adds nothing of its own. Then the two are equal. Kaivalya comes from kevala: alone, only, whole. Not loneliness. More like standing on its own, needing nothing. The seer, no longer tangled with what it sees. Then the classical commentary adds a line that's easy to miss. This freedom comes whether or not someone has the powers. Fifteen days of invisibility, elephants, gods at the door, and none of it was required. A plain person with a clear mind arrives at the same place. Now look back over book three. Concentration, meditation, absorption. Prajna, samyama, the mind's transformations. Then the powers: past and future, other minds, strength, the stars, the heart. The warning in the middle. The elements, the senses, omniscience let go, the gods refused, the instant seen clearly. And at the end, not a greater power, but a cleaner window. Tomorrow, the fourth and last book, on freedom itself.

segments.voice: Rest on the breath and notice what the mind is adding right now: a mood, a commentary, a judgment about how this is going. Don't fight it; see it as a smudge on the glass, and let it fade on its own. Then look through again at the breath, plain and clear.
Kaivalya. Aloneness, wholeness, freedom: when the mind's clarity is equal to the seer's purity.
Your line: equal. A clean window, with or without any of the powers. Book three, done.

480.title: The powers by birth, herbs, mantra, discipline, samadhi (4.1)
480.hook: the last book opens by listing five places powers can come from, and only one of them is samadhi
480.howItsDone: Hindu traditions recognize many sources of extraordinary ability, including birth, medicinal preparations, mantra and austerity, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras use 4.1 to remind students that such abilities are not in themselves signs of liberation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kaivalya, and your line, equal. When the mind is as clear as the seer, freedom comes, with or without the powers.

A hummingbird hangs in the air outside a kitchen window, perfectly still, wings a blur. No human being has ever done that on their own. And the hummingbird never meditated a day in its life. It didn't fast, chant or study. It was born that way. Hold onto that bird. Book four of the Yoga Sutras, the last and shortest, is called Kaivalya, freedom. Its very first sutra is about where powers come from, and the hummingbird is the first answer.
screen: `A HUMMINGBIRD HOVERS.` → `IT NEVER MEDITATED.` → `BORN THAT WAY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.1: the powers are born of birth, herbs, mantra, discipline or samadhi. Five sources. Birth: some abilities come with the body you're born into; the classical commentary speaks of powers that come with birth into another kind of body. A bird is born to fly. Herbs: the commentary mentions elixirs, said to be found in the realms of the asuras. Mantra: sacred sound, recited with power. Discipline, tapas: the heat of austerity. And samadhi: everything book three described. Why does the book of freedom open here? One answer: it puts the powers in their place. If an ability can come from birth, or from an herb, then an ability on its own proves nothing about someone's inner life. A hummingbird hovers, and nobody calls it enlightened. Patanjali has already called the powers obstacles in samadhi. Here he adds that they aren't even unique to yoga. Five doors lead to them, and only one is samadhi. Over the next few sutras, he'll say the mind born of meditation is the one that leaves no new karma behind. So the list isn't a menu. It's a quiet sorting. Book four is short, thirty-four sutras, and it's headed somewhere bigger than any power: mind, karma, time, and finally freedom itself. But first it clears the table. Five sources, and none of them is the point.

segments.voice: Feel the breath come without your effort; it's a gift of birth you never earned. Then think of one ability you never really worked for, a good ear, a quick laugh, patience with children, and hold it lightly: no pride, no dismissing it, just this came with me.
Kaivalya, freedom, the name of the Yoga Sutras' fourth book. Its first sutra names five sources of power: birth, herbs, mantra, discipline and samadhi.
Your line: five sources. Only one of the five doors is samadhi. See you tomorrow.

481.title: The mind's transformations from nature (4.2–4.6)
481.hook: real change comes from nature overflowing, and practice doesn't push the water, it only breaks the dam, like a farmer opening a channel
481.tomorrow: Karma of the yogi — neither white nor black
481.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often use the farmer of 4.3 to describe practice as removing obstacles rather than producing results, and some Hindus describe their discipline and worship in the same way, as clearing the way for grace or for what is already within.

segments.voice: Yesterday: book four opened with five sources of power, birth, herbs, mantra, discipline and samadhi. A power alone proves nothing.

Early morning on a farm. The canal is full, and water sits behind a low wall of packed earth at the head of a dry field. The farmer doesn't carry the water over in buckets; he'd never finish. He takes one spade, cuts the little earthen wall, and steps back. The water runs down every furrow on its own, because water runs downhill. One cut. Patanjali chose this farmer, of all the pictures in the world, to explain how a person changes.
screen: `A FULL CANAL.` → `ONE CUT IN THE EARTH WALL.` → `THE WATER DOES THE REST.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.2: the transformation into another kind of being comes from the overflowing of nature. Prakriti, nature, is already full of potential, like the canal; change is that fullness flowing into a new shape. Then sutra 4.3, the farmer. The instrumental cause doesn't set nature moving. It only pierces the barrier, like a farmer. The instrumental cause means everything you do: good deeds, practice, discipline. None of it pushes nature anywhere. Nature does its own flowing. What practice can do is cut the wall. The classical commentary spells it out: the farmer who wants to flood one field from another doesn't drag the water by hand. He breaks the dike, and the water flows in by itself. So in a person, practice removes what's in the way, and nature's own fullness runs in. Then the sutras turn to a strange idea. Sutra 4.4: a yogi can form minds, made from I-ness alone. Sutra 4.5: one mind directs the many in their different tasks. And 4.6: of all these minds, the one born of meditation leaves no residue, no new seeds for the storehouse. More on that thread tomorrow. For today, stay with the farmer. It's a gentle picture of effort. You aren't making the water. You're finding the wall, cutting it, and stepping back.

segments.voice: Rest on the breath and notice whether you're pushing anything: the breath, the stillness, the feeling of doing this right. Look instead for what's in the way, tight shoulders, a clenched jaw, and let one of them gently open. Then step back, like the farmer, and let the breath run through on its own.
Kshetrika, the farmer. Change flows from nature's own fullness; practice, like a farmer, only removes the barrier.
Your line: the farmer removes the barrier. The canal was already full. Day four hundred eighty-one, done.

482.title: Karma of the yogi — neither white nor black (4.7)
482.hook: most people's actions come in three colors; Patanjali says the yogi's come in none
482.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often read 4.7 alongside the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action without attachment to its fruit, and some practitioners try to do service quietly, without seeking credit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kshetrika, the farmer. Practice doesn't push the water; it opens the wall, and nature flows.

Laundry day. Three piles on the bedroom floor: the whites, the darks, and the mixed heap that's a bit of both. Everything goes somewhere. Patanjali sorts human action the same way, by color, and he names the piles. Then, in one short line of the fourth chapter, he says the action of someone who has gone all the way in yoga goes in no pile at all.
screen: `THREE PILES ON THE FLOOR.` → `ACTION, SORTED BY COLOR.` → `AND ONE KIND IN NO PILE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.7: karma ashukla-akrishnam yoginas, trividham itaresham. The action of the yogi is not white and not black. For everyone else, it is of three kinds. Shukla means white, or bright. Krishna here means black, or dark. The old commentary attributed to Vyasa spells out the three. Black is action that harms. Mixed, black-and-white, is ordinary action: it does good, but it leans on outward means and touches others, so it's never perfectly clean. White is action done inwardly, through discipline, study and meditation. All three leave seeds, bright or dark, and seeds sprout. That's the surprise: for Patanjali, white karma isn't the finish line. A gold chain still holds you. So what is the fourth kind, neither white nor black? The commentators describe someone whose afflictions have worn thin, who acts without craving the fruit. The act still happens. Food gets cooked, the sick get visited. But nothing new is sown, because nobody is standing there waiting for the harvest. It's close to what Krishna tells Arjuna in the Gita: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. So the line isn't saying the yogi stops caring about good and harm. The yogi's good is done without a hand held out.

483.title: Desires are beginningless (4.10–4.11)
483.hook: you can't find the first craving, and Patanjali says you don't need to
483.tomorrow: The object exists independent of the mind (4.14–4.17)
483.howItsDone: In the yoga tradition, vasanas are worked with less by searching for their origin than by withdrawing what sustains them: practice, non-attachment and discernment, as the earlier chapters of the Yoga Sutras teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashukla-akrishna, action neither white nor black, done free of its fruit.

It's eleven at night and you're standing at the open fridge, not hungry, looking for something. Or scrolling, thumb moving on its own. A familiar question shows up: why am I like this? When did this start? Childhood, a hard year, something someone said? We dig for the first cause as if finding it would switch the whole thing off. Patanjali's answer is short, almost blunt. There is no first one.

segments.voice: Sutra 4.10: tasam anaditvam chashisho nityatvat. And they have no beginning, because the will to live is everlasting. They are the vasanas, the deep traces of desire laid down by past action. The commentary points to something anyone can see: every creature, from its first breath, wants to go on. Let me not stop being. That wish has no start date, so the traces it lays down have none either. If there's no first craving, there's no one moment to blame, and no point spending years in the archive. Then sutra 4.11 turns the key. These traces are held together by four things: a cause, a result, a place to rest in the mind, and an object to lean on. Take those away and the traces go too. A campfire can burn for as long as anyone remembers, and nobody knows who lit it. It still goes out when the wood stops coming. So the practice isn't archaeology. It's noticing what feeds the craving right now. Now the week, from the top. Omniscience offered, and the gods' invitation refused. Discernment down to the instant. Kaivalya, when the mind's purity equals the self's. The five sources of powers. The farmer opening the channel. Action neither white nor black. And today: desires without a beginning, which can still have an end.

Vasana, the trace desire leaves behind. These traces have no first moment, because the will to live has none, but they rest on supports, and without them they fall away.
Your line: no beginning. But even a very old fire still needs wood. A week, done.
